title: Block close: one river
hook: the streams differ; the people remains

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: responsible for one another. Arevim, guarantors, like Judah standing behind Benjamin. Whose stumble did you put your hand behind? Today, we close the block on the movements. Day one thousand two hundred fifty.

"And a river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from thence it was parted, and became into four heads." That's the second chapter of Genesis. One river, rising in one place, splitting into branches that run off toward different lands. The text gives each branch a name. It never says one branch is the real river and the others are leaks. We began this block with a carry that said many streams. We end it with that picture from Eden, borrowed as an image, not as a proof. Today we walk the whole block once, from the source to the branches.
screen: `A RIVER WENT OUT OF EDEN.` → `PARTED INTO HEADS.` → `EACH BRANCH HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: Block close. Turn it four ways. First, what they share and what they debate. We started there: one Torah, one history, and real questions about how the law binds and who decides. Second, the streams themselves. Orthodox, with its binding tradition, and inside it Haredi devotion to study, Modern Orthodoxy holding Torah and the world, Religious Zionism, Sephardi and Mizrahi homes, Chabad's open doors, and new roles for women. Conservative, or Masorti, with its law that develops and its egalitarian prayer. Reform, from the early platform to the return to ritual and the prophetic call. Reconstructionist, deciding together. Then Renewal, Humanistic Judaism, secular Jews, the Karaites who are still here, and in Israel, hiloni, masorti, dati. Third, the hard edges. Who is a Jew, and whose conversion counts: the streams give different answers, and we said so plainly. Fourth, what holds it together. The traditional middle, Jews with no label, lay-led rooms. Shared ethics: tzedakah, kindness, justice. Hillel and Shammai, disagreeing for the sake of heaven and still marrying into each other's families. Klal Yisrael, the whole people. Ahavat Yisrael, love that doesn't wait. Visiting as a guest. Choosing where you belong. And arevim, all Israel guarantors for one another. None of this ranks the branches. In Genesis the river waters the garden, and from there it parts and runs on toward other lands, each branch carrying water from the same source. Tomorrow a new block begins, and it turns inward: Mussar, the slow work on one's own character.
screen: `WHAT THEY SHARE, WHAT THEY DEBATE.` · `THE STREAMS, ONE BY ONE.` · `THE HARD EDGES, SAID PLAINLY.` · `WHAT HOLDS IT TOGETHER.` · then, large: `MANY STREAMS, ONE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one kind thing about another stream. Settle, and breathe. Pick a branch of the river that isn't yours, or isn't the one you lean toward. It might be one you've argued with. Find one thing in it that you can honestly admire: a melody, a kind of devotion, a way of welcoming, a question it keeps asking. Put it into one sentence. Say it silently a few times until it sounds true. If you're not Jewish, do the same for a group in your own tradition or town you usually keep at a distance. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Block close. The end of our walk through the movements: many streams, real differences, one people, like the river that went out of Eden and parted into heads. Today's word.
Your line: many streams, one river. Today, say your one kind sentence out loud to someone, about a stream that isn't yours. Day one thousand two hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Jews from different movements meet in shared institutions, community events and family celebrations, and joint study and service projects bring members of several streams together.
